Yes. Reta, Triple G and GLP-3 are all nicknames for the same molecule: retatrutide, an investigational weight-loss drug developed by Eli Lilly. None of them is an official brand name.

Each nickname comes from a different place. “Reta” is a short form of the name. “Triple G” refers to the three hormones the drug copies. “GLP-3” is a media label that Lilly itself calls scientifically inaccurate, because there is no hormone called GLP-3.

Below, we explain where each name comes from, why “GLP-3” misleads, and what the names do and do not tell you.

What is retatrutide (LY3437943)?

Every nickname in this article points back to one molecule. Retatrutide is its official international name, and the code in the heading is the research code Lilly gave it during development. You will see that code in clinical trial records and scientific papers.

Retatrutide is a GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon receptor agonist. In plain terms, one molecule acts on three hormone receptors that help control appetite, blood sugar and how much energy the body uses. It is given as a once-weekly injection and has been tested in Lilly’s TRIUMPH phase 3 programme.

We cover what retatrutide is and what the trials found in our longer guide. Here, the focus is on the names.

What does each name mean?

The three nicknames grew up in different places: online shorthand, news coverage and seller listings. All of them describe retatrutide; they just describe it differently.

Reta: a short form of the name

“Reta” is the first four letters of retatrutide. It is the easiest name to type and say, so it is common in online discussions, social media posts and product listings. You may also see “reta peptide”, which is one of the most searched forms of the name. It carries no extra meaning beyond the shortened name itself.

Triple G: three hormones in one

“Triple G” refers to the three hormones retatrutide imitates: GLP-1, GIP and glucagon. News outlets use it too: when Lilly reported its TRIUMPH-4 results in December 2025, ABC’s Good Morning America described retatrutide as a drug “dubbed triple G”. It is also written “Triple-G”. Of the three nicknames, it is the closest to what the drug actually does.

GLP-3, GLP-3 RT and GLP-3 RTA: number-based labels

“GLP-3” appeared in headlines as a quick way to say “one step beyond GLP-1 drugs”. Scientific American, for example, called retatrutide an “experimental GLP-3 weight-loss drug”. Sellers then built codes on top of it, adding letters from the name: retatrutide is sometimes sold as “GLP-3 RT”, “GLP-3 Reta”, “GLP-3 RET” or “GLP-3 RTA”. All of these refer to retatrutide, but the “GLP-3” part is the one name in this list that is scientifically wrong.

Why is “GLP-3” a misleading name?

There is no hormone called GLP-3. Lilly’s own explainer, updated in October 2026, calls “GLP-3” a scientifically inaccurate label used informally in the media, and suggests “triple agonist” as the better description.

The number is part of a hormone’s name, not a count

The “1” in GLP-1 does not mean one hormone. GLP-1 stands for glucagon-like peptide-1, the full name of a single natural hormone. Counting up from it to “GLP-3” mixes a hormone’s name with a number of receptors, which is where the confusion starts.

GLP-2 is a different hormone altogether

Glucagon-like peptide-2 is a real hormone, but it works on the gut lining, not on appetite. Medicines that copy it, such as teduglutide, are used for short bowel syndrome, not for weight loss. So a “GLP-2” label on tirzepatide is just as misleading as “GLP-3” on retatrutide.

How the three drugs line up

The clearer way to compare these drugs is by the receptors they act on:

Drug Receptors it acts on Nicknames you may see Status
Semaglutide GLP-1 “sema”, “GLP-1 SMA” Approved (sold as Ozempic and Wegovy)
Tirzepatide GIP and GLP-1 “tirz”, “GLP-2 TRZ” Approved (sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound)
Retatrutide GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon “reta”, “Triple G”, “GLP-3 RT” Investigational, not yet approved

Read this way, the pattern is simple: one, two and three receptors. That is what the numbered codes are trying to say, even though the GLP-2 and GLP-3 labels borrow names that mean something else in biology.

Do different names mean different products?

No. Reta, Triple G and the GLP-3 codes all name the same molecule. A different nickname on a listing does not mean a different compound, a stronger version or a newer formula.

What a nickname cannot tell you is who made the product or what exactly is in the vial. For research buyers, the details that matter are on the label and the paperwork:

  • the full name, retatrutide, not only a nickname
  • the amount per vial
  • a batch or lot number
  • a certificate of analysis for that batch
  • a clear “research use only” statement

We supply retatrutide in Bali as a research compound. Our retatrutide is sold for research use only. It is not a Lilly product, it is not a BPOM-registered medicine, and it is not approved for human use.

Is retatrutide approved under any of these names?

No. Retatrutide is not yet approved as a medicine under any name, official or informal.

Where retatrutide stands in 2026

Lilly has finished the main phase 3 obesity trials and says its data package is complete. It plans to submit retatrutide to the US Food and Drug Administration in the first quarter of 2027. In Indonesia, BPOM would review it separately. Until then, retatrutide is available in Bali as a research compound, supplied for research use only.

Will retatrutide get a brand name?

Most likely, yes, but only once it is approved. Approved medicines get a brand name for sale: tirzepatide is sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound, and semaglutide as Ozempic and Wegovy. No brand name has been approved for retatrutide, because the drug itself has not been approved. Reta, Triple G and GLP-3 are nicknames, not brands.

Conclusion

Reta, Triple G and GLP-3 are the same thing: three nicknames for retatrutide, Lilly’s GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon receptor agonist. “Reta” shortens the name, “Triple G” points to its three hormones, and “GLP-3” is a media label that Lilly calls scientifically inaccurate, because no GLP-3 hormone exists. Codes such as GLP-3 RT and GLP-3 RTA build on that label.

A nickname tells you which molecule a listing claims, but not who made it or what is in the vial, so the label details matter more than the name. Retatrutide has no approved brand name yet, because it is not yet approved as a medicine; Lilly plans to file with the FDA in early 2027. Until then, it is available in Bali as a research compound, supplied for research use only.

Frequently asked questions

Is reta the same as retatrutide?

Yes. “Reta” is simply a short form of retatrutide. A product called “reta” or “reta peptide” is claiming to contain retatrutide.

Why is retatrutide called Triple G?

Because it imitates three hormones: GLP-1, GIP and glucagon. The nickname has appeared in news coverage of Lilly’s trial results.

What does GLP-3 RT mean?

It is a seller code for retatrutide. “GLP-3” is an informal label for a drug acting on three receptors, and “RT” comes from the name retatrutide. Similar codes include GLP-3 Reta, GLP-3 RET and GLP-3 RTA.

Is a triple agonist the same as a GLP-3?

Yes, in the way the terms are used. “Triple agonist” is the accurate description of a drug that acts on three receptors, and it is the term Lilly recommends. “GLP-3” is the informal label for the same idea.

Is retatrutide a peptide?

Yes. Retatrutide is a synthetic peptide, like semaglutide and tirzepatide, which is why it is often searched as “retatrutide peptide” or “reta peptide”.

Is retatrutide the same as tirzepatide?

No. They are different molecules from the same company. Tirzepatide acts on two receptors, GIP and GLP-1, and is approved as Mounjaro and Zepbound. Retatrutide adds a third, glucagon, and is still investigational.
